newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Baht devaluation is no economic cure-all - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Baht devaluation is no economic cure-all - analysts.

text.p: In a market still awash with talk of an imminent Thai baht devaluation, analysts took a step back on Friday to look at the impact and potential problems an officially sanctioned drop in the value of the currency may bring.
They certainly do not see it as a cure-all.

Speculators who were burned by the Bank of Thailand's imposition of controls to restrict baht outflows saw a bright new day dawning with the resignation on Thursday of hard-line finance minister Amnuay Viravan, although the Bank of Thailand again stressed there would be no devaluation.
Devaluation is not the paliative it may seem at first glance and analysts said it was doubtful it would even allow interest rates to come down in the near term.

With a current account deficit around six percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP), any lessening of the central banks resolve would probably lead to a further capital outflow and rates would have to be kept high or raised to prevent a currency meltdown, they said.

"A 10 to 20 percent drop in the value of the currency, which are the sort of numbers being banded around in the market, would not go down at all well with firms and finance houses with unhedged overseas debts," said Kobus Van Der Wath, regional head of treasury economics at Standard Chartered in Singapore.
It is also questionable whether Thailand urgently needs to boost exports by devaluing and making its goods cheaper overseas. Some analysts are already looking for a rise in export growth this year.

It would also give a sharp prod to import price inflation although, as with Britain after the 1992 sterling crisis, a surge in imports prices can be kept under control if domestic demand is not racing away, and it certainly is not in Thailand.

But the main reason the Thai authorities do not want to give into a devalution is that they do not want to increase the debt burden of ailing firms, particularly in the financial sector, given the very high level of off-shore debt.

Last week's announcement by Bank of Thailand assistant governor Siri Ganjarerndee that Thailand would adopt a Singapore style foreign exchange regime is seen as flawed as a long-term policy simply because Thailand has a current account deficit and Singapore a surplus.

"Overseas investment is needed to fund the deficit so deterring foreign investment by imposing a rock-hard exchange rate scheme so investors have no flexibility is not much of an option'" said one analyst at a European bank here.

"The fundamentals haven't changed and corporates remain weak from the overseas liabilities burden so a devaluation now would cure nothing at all," said Chiang Yao Chye, economist at CIBC Wood Gundy in Singapore.
Nevertheless that does not mean that the baht should not eventually be allowed to find it own level, which analysts say is essential if Thailand wants to attract sustained and long-term fund flows.
So what of the future and what is in store for the baht assuming the Thai authorities and central bank do stand their ground for now?

Some analysts believe Thailand will eventually tend to move towards a more flexible exchange rate policy and one way to achieve that would be to widen the official band in which the onshore baht is allowed to trade.

At present the Exchange Equalization Fund (EEF), under the Bank of Thailand, announces a daily fixing for US$/baht with a spread of four satangs at which it stands ready to buy or sell from resident banks.
Widening this band at present would simply result in a de facto devalution given the current lack of confidence and poor background economic fundamentals.

But further down the road -- perhaps much further, analysts are talking in terms of several months and more -- it would help bring about more flexibility and allow Thailand to achieve its plan to become a financal centre as well as to promote the baht as a regional currency.

"I think they will ultimately move to make the baht more flexible and one way to do that would be to widen the band...I really don't think the Bank of Thailand or the government see outright devaluation as an option," CIBC's Chye said.
